title: El café
goal: Order food and drink in a café or restaurant, ask for the bill and understand prices up to 100.

lessons.title: Something to drink
lessons.notes:
To order, **quiero** (I want) is normal and not rude in Spanish - your **por favor** does the politeness. **Quisiera** (I would like) is a touch more polite, good with waiters and in shops.
**Quiero un café, por favor. Quisiera un té.**
Ask a friend **¿Quieres...?** (do you want...?).
**Con** = with, **sin** = without: **un café con leche** (a white coffee), **un té sin azúcar**. **De** tells you what's inside: **un vaso de agua** (a glass of water), **una taza de té**.
Latin America drinks **jugo**; Spain drinks **zumo**.

items.note: A little more polite than quiero.
With an accent: 'te' without one means 'you' (te llamas).

sentences.es: Quiero un café con leche, por favor.
sentences.en: I'd like a white coffee, please.
accept_en: I want a coffee with milk, please.
I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

sentences.en: I would like a tea without sugar.
accept_en: I'd like a tea with no sugar.

lessons.title: Something to eat
lessons.notes:
Spanish builds 'X sandwich' backwards with **de**: **un sándwich de jamón** (a ham sandwich), **una sopa de pollo** (chicken soup), **un jugo de naranja**. The main thing first, then 'of' what.
Food that's good to eat right now is **está bueno / buena** (estar - it tastes good today): **La sopa está muy buena.** Ser bueno would mean it's healthy or good quality in general.
**¿Algo más?** (anything else?) - you'll hear it after every order. **Algo** = something; **más** = more.

sentences.es: Quisiera un sándwich de jamón y queso.
sentences.en: I'd like a ham and cheese sandwich.

lessons.title: At the restaurant
lessons.notes:
Some set phrases do most of the work:
**Una mesa para dos, por favor.** (a table for two)
**¿Me trae el menú?** - literally 'do you bring me the menu?', a polite request.
**Para mí, el pollo.** (for me, the chicken)
**La cuenta, por favor.** (the bill)
**Para** = for. **Rico** describes tasty food: **¡Está muy rico!**
Waiter: **el mesero / la mesera** in Mexico and much of Latin America, **el camarero / la camarera** in Spain. Spain also calls the menu **la carta**. Tipping is expected in Mexico (about 10-15%) and much less fixed elsewhere.

items.note: Spain: el camarero. Argentina: el mozo.

sentences.es: Una mesa para dos, por favor.

sentences.en: Could you bring me the menu, please?
accept_en: Can I have the menu, please?
Can you bring me the menu, please?
Can I have the bill, please?
In Mexico people leave a tip.

lessons.title: Numbers to 100 and prices
lessons.notes:
The tens: **treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa** - and **cien** (100).
**21-29** are written as one word: **veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés...** (veinte + y + uno run together); before a masculine noun uno drops its -o: **veintiún años**.
From **31** you use **y** as a separate word: **treinta y cinco** (35), **noventa y nueve** (99).
Prices: **¿Cuánto cuesta?** (how much does it cost?) - **Cuesta cinco dólares.** For several things: **cuestan**. Or simply **Son cincuenta pesos** (that's fifty pesos).

items.note: veintiún before a masculine noun: veintiún años.

accept_en: How much does the coffee cost?

sentences.es: La cuenta es de cincuenta dólares.
accept_en: The bill comes to fifty dollars.
My grandfather is eighty years old.

sentences.es: El vino cuesta treinta y cinco dólares.
Mi abuela tiene setenta y dos años.
accept_en: My grandmother is seventy-two years old.
